title.narrative: Support to NRC Consortium under the Resilience and Adaptation Fund (RAF)

description.narrative:
Activities Under Output 1.1:
Activity 1: Vulnerable refugees and host community farmers practice Climate Smart Agriculture and Climate-Smart Livestock rearing to build resilient livelihoods. The project will select food-insecure households among the host and refugee communities, prioritising women-headed households, pregnant and lactating women and households with elderly and/or people with disabilities and ensuring that households who have access to small land are included in the selection. Households will be trained on Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices for homestead food production, focusing on diversified and nutritious foods and vertical nutrition gardening (due to the absence of agricultural land in the camps). The farmers will receive training on resilient crop varieties, soil health, efficient irrigation, and integrated pest management. Furthermore, some families in the camps will be supported in fish farming. Host community members will receive climate-smart livestock training delivered by a private sector company collaborating with the project and which will include improved livestock-housing, feed, and animal health practices. Both host community and refugees’ beneficiaries will be supported with In-kind inputs (toolkits and input support).
In host communities, drought-resistant and saline-tolerant seeds for high-value but low-volume vegetable, spice and grain crops will be provided, as well as support to poultry and fish farming at individual and community level. In camps. To build strong market connections, the project will establish collections and market centres to support farmers and their groups to sell their surplus produce to WFP fresh food vendors. Some products will also be sold out in the local market in Ukhiya and Cox’s Bazar. HI will work closely with consortium partners to identify and address accessibility barriers in collection points, training sites, and market centres. Additionally, HI will also refer persons with disabilities and their caregivers to be part of this activity and provide them with tailored assistive devices and adaptive tools to meaningfully engage in this activity. This approach will ensure that persons with disabilities and their caregivers can actively participate in DRC-supported agricultural value chains across camps and host communities.
Activity 2: Rohingya refugee and their host community women’s economic empowerment creating ‘Green Jobs’ by recycling readymade garment industry waste. Within the scope of the circular economy, DRC and local partner EDSO have installed eight Ready-Made Garment (RMG) industry waste recycling centres (four in Rohingya camps and four in host communities), provided training (24 days), tools and accessories to 100 women (50 Rohingya and 50 host), and employed them to produce floor mats, door mats and other marketable products using the recycled RMG industry waste, locally called ‘jhoot’. This has been an attractive business for both Rohingya and host community women since each earns $3-5 per day through this employment.
Through the RAF project, DRC will work with its partner ESDO and the already established groups to expand the scope of this intervention and seek to strengthen market linkages. DRC will provide advanced level skills training (level 1 and 2) to 100 women to enable them to produce finer and higher-quality recycled products with greater market potential, and to build their skills as training facilitators to train additional camp and host community members. DRC will provide the required tools and accessories to the trained women to repair and maintain the existing eight recycling centres, as well as supporting them to install eight additional recycling centres in camps and host communities. DRC will collect textile leftovers from RMG industries and deliver this to the centres for the women to recycle and reuse them to produce floormats, doormats and other marketable products. To advance market linkages, DRC will establish one sales outlet in Cox’s Bazar, which will be an expansion of the already established and successful sales outlet in Ukhiya sub district. DRC has an informal set up with a private company KDS Group and Accessories in Chittagong who provides ‘jhoot’ to DRC recycling centres. DRC will seek to formalise a tripartite MoU (DRC- KDS Group – CBOs) for the sustainable supply of the ‘jhoot” for the recycling. DRC will continue RMG industry waste engaging with private companies after the project period through Danida funding.
Activity3: Facilitate and strengthen market and service linkages with private companies, buyers and suppliers to improve access to climate smart information, digital technologies and financial services. The IRC will facilitate linkages between value-chain actors and strengthen the enabling environment by providing market information to farmers and livestock owners, market and service linkages with private companies, buyers, and suppliers to enhance access to climate-smart information, technologies, and financial services (for host communities). The IRC will collaborate with a livestock service provider to deliver innovative cattle identification technology to facilitate farmers’ access to livestock insurance. The insurance will support farmers in accessing real-time data, ensure vaccination is updated to secure payouts in the event of livestock illness or loss. In coordination with LSDS, IRC will pilot the formalisation of refugee-owned microenterprises by supporting the identification of market-viable businesses, enhancing skills, and linking refugees with host-community buyers and suppliers. The pilot will provide training, input support, record-keeping assistance, and improved market access. Lessons learned from this initiative will inform an Approach to Scale for the sustainable formalisation of camp-based businesses.
Activity: 4: Vulnerable refugees and host community youths and women acquire market-relevant Skills (including green skills) and diversify their livelihoods and income generating sources. The project conducts an assessment to identify market-driven green skills and livelihoods opportunities most useful for the economically vulnerable refugees and host community youth and women.
Clients will be enrolled in financial literacy and business skills training. The modules will be contextualized and consulted with the LSDS sector, accommodating the learning from other partners to increase business skills, entrepreneurship, business planning, financial record keeping, market analysis and product supply chain of the clients. The consortium partners have been delivering these trainings in Bangladesh since 2022, with results showing that 90% of the host community clients have increased their monthly income from baseline to endline. Clients will also be enrolled in Green Skills trainings on occupations, such as waste management, organic composting, gas stove repair, solar installation and maintenance, alongside demand-driven trades like- soap production, plumbing and WASH facility maintenance. Handicrafts and hand stitching (including boutique and block) and training on digital skills will also be included. The project will facilitate linkages with private sector on the development of the Green Skills training and in facilitating scoping for employment or self-employment opportunities for the host community. To support starting up green businesses, the successfully trained participants will receive training toolkits in the refugee camp and start-up inputs and support in the host community. The project will facilitate market linkage meetings among the host community producers, buyers and input suppliers. As an active member of the LSDS, and with the support of the wider consortium members, the project will also collaborate with camp authorities to pilot a formalisation activity for refugee-owned microenterprise, linking them with buyers and suppliers to broaden market access for refugees, contingent on the approval of CiCs and higher level authorities, initially strengthening market linkages within the camps, and adapting this with learning and advocacy to include the host community as much as feasible. This project aims for scalable incremental strides in challenging some of the policy restrictions on refugee livelihoods in this protracted crisis.
HI will complement these efforts by directly implementing inclusive vocational training targeting persons with disabilities and their caregivers. Building on its experience in disability-inclusive skills development, HI will also support consortium partners in making training environments physically accessible and in providing adapted tools and reasonable accommodations to enable equitable participation. In collaboration with its partner PROTTASHY, HI will facilitate market linkages by showcasing participant products through retail outlets such as Prottashyi’s Cox’s Bazar Shop and online platforms, supporting the launch of home-based microenterprises and helping sustain income generation beyond the project period. This intervention complements the project’s broader skills training by providing an inclusive entry point into green livelihoods for individuals often excluded from mainstream economic opportunities.
Activity 5: Improve interpersonal and life skills among targeted youth, equipping them with the critical soft skills needed to navigate the labour market, build social capital and lead social initiatives. This activity integrates NRC’s life skills modules into vocational training programmes to equip youth with personal development, leadership, and community engagement skills. The aim is to foster youth-led, community-driven solutions that strengthen social cohesion and resilience. In addition, climate education components will be embedded to raise awareness and promote adaptive behaviours, enabling young people to become proactive agents of change in the face of climate-related challenges.
Activity 6: Enhance market transition support through mentoring, job placements, and provision of start-up inputs (cash and in-kind), facilitating direct entry into income-generating opportunities. The vocational training participants (Youth with and without disability and other vulnerable groups) will be supported through structured apprenticeship placements and coaching-mentoring initiatives to gain hands-on training and attainment of practical skills in relevant trades. These opportunities will enhance employability, support income generation, and promote long-term self-reliance. This approach bridges the gap between training and the job market, empowering youth and other vulnerable groups to transition into sustainable livelihoods.
In addition, upon successful completion of vocational training, participants (With and without disability) will receive tailored business start-up kits or start-up capital to launch home-based enterprises or micro-businesses and job placement support to enable employment and self-employment through private sector engagement. If the government does not allow cash support for this activity, partners will provide start-up kits and other inputs to support the beneficiaries’ business ideas. These kits will enable trainees to apply their newly acquired skills in income-generating activities, fostering entrepreneurship and economic self-reliance. This initiative aims to reduce long-term aid dependency by promoting sustainable livelihoods and empowering youth, persons with disabilities and marginalized groups as drivers of local economic resilience.
Activity 7: Strengthen youth capacity in entrepreneurship and financial literacy, supporting the development of small and medium businesses and improved financial decision-making at the household level. The programme aims to strengthen youth capacity in entrepreneurship and financial literacy by equipping them with the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed to start and manage small and medium businesses. Through targeted training and mentorship, young people will be supported to identify viable business opportunities, develop business plans, and make informed financial decisions. This will not only enhance their individual economic prospects but also contribute to improved financial decision-making at the household level, promoting greater resilience and self-reliance within communities. These sessions will be integrated in the skills development programme and target all enrolled youth.
Activity 8: Pilot Workshop for Repair, Recycling, and Local Production of Assistive Devices and Consumables HI will pilot a localised workshop model in Cox’s Bazar to support the repair, refurbishment, and recycling of assistive devices, while also exploring the low-cost, small-scale production of therapeutic consumables and materials. The initiative will focus on restoring the functionality of worn or damaged assistive devices—such as mobility aids, crutches, or wheelchairs—through repair or component reuse, reducing waste and increasing device availability. This approach promotes environmental sustainability and aligns with circular economic principles.
The workshop will also test locally sourced production of high-demand consumables (e.g., positioning cushions, adaptive grips, therapy tools), using affordable, climate-appropriate materials to enhance the long-term availability and affordability of essential items. HI will identify and train a cohort of skilled youth, including persons with disabilities, in basic repair, adaptation, and production techniques, contributing to inclusive green livelihoods and skill development. This pilot aims to serve as a scalable model for climate-smart, inclusive service delivery and may inform future engagement with private sector actors or social enterprises to promote sustainability beyond the project period. Additionally, to support the meaningful participation of persons with disabilities across project activities, HI will facilitate access to assistive devices and functional support through referral and coordination with its ongoing rehabilitation programmes. HI will leverage its existing static service points and technical teams to provide functional assessments, home-based therapy, provision of assistive devices, and reasonable accommodation support including tool adaptations where needed. This support will enable individuals to fully engage in livelihood training, household preparedness, awareness campaigns, DRR planning, and the use of accessible infrastructure.
Activities Under Output 1.2:
Activity 1: Capacity building of the Rohingya refugee and host community on the climate adaptation and restoration of degraded environment through training and community led micro projects. In line with the DRC’s localisation strategy, DRC has established and been working with 54 CBOs (both Rohingya led, and host community led) aiming to empower community-based organisations in climate adaptation, mitigation, and mainstreaming. Through the RAF, DRC will work with the already established CBOs to provide climate adaptation and mitigation training and support the CBOs to design and implement their micro- community led projects (CLPs). DRC will provide business start-up and continuity support in cash, in kind and technical support to the CBOs and community groups (both registered and non- registered). Some examples of CLPs are climate smart agriculture including vertical gardening in the camps, community led climate resilient livelihood initiatives, household level climate disaster risks mitigation works, vermi- composting, climate farmers field school, based on their needs and technical feasibilities. This has been proven to be a very effective and sustainable approach to building resilience at the community level in the Cox’s Bazar context. DRC will implement the activity based on its experience in the field level benefiting 1,625 unique beneficiaries.
Activity 2: Community-led climate resilience interventions through Nature-Based Solutions by engaging Rohingya and host community men and women. In collaboration with Site Management (DRC) and Site Development (IOM) leads, DRC, HI and IRC will select disaster-prone and climate impacted sites for development of local adaptation plans (in six camps and two host communities) and repair and upgrade works, to mitigate the risks associated with climate related shocks and stresses and directly contribute to disaster risk reduction, and community infrastructure development. Community-led local adaptation plans will be developed, with orientation support provided to mobilise Rohingya and host community members, including men, women, and persons with disabilities, to participate in climate resilience initiatives. The plans will outline required repair and upgrade works, taking a nature-based solutions approach, including shelters, schools, and community facilities, as well as irrigation canals, drainage systems, protective embankments, and raised seedbeds. In total, 2,290 individuals (56% female and 44% male) will be involved in the process for NbS solutions. This consist of1,100 individuals from host communities and 1,190 refugees, among them 700 persons with disabilities and their caregivers
To secure community leadership and involvement in the works, a cash-for-work (CfW) modality will be adopted whereby camp and community members, including persons with disabilities or caregivers, will directly contribute to the repair and upgrading works. Additional activities will be included such as tree planting, slope stabilisation through ecosystem-based adaptation (e.g. vegetation for slope stabilisation) and ecosystem restoration, to enhance the natural resilience of the surrounding environment and thereby reduce the risks of erosion, flooding, and heat stress. Furthermore, linkages will be established with Materials Recovery Facilities, a youth-led waste management system, to transform camp waste into high-quality compost and marketable products.
Repairing and upgrading essential community and market infrastructure through a disability inclusive CfW modality will improve access to services, markets, and livelihoods, ensuring that communities are better equipped to absorb, adapt to, and recover from future climate-related shocks. CfW plays a critical role in strengthening the resilience of vulnerable communities by linking immediate income support with long-term climate adaptation measures. Overall, the efforts included in this activity aim to reduce environmental degradation, enhance community livelihoods, and mitigate social vulnerabilities. By fostering community ownership and reducing reliance on harmful coping strategies, the project contributes to long-term resilience and decreased dependency on humanitarian aid.
Activity 3: Develop Local Adaptation Plans and Actions (LAPAs) in collaboration with communities and local government to address climate risks and promote resilient livelihoods: In support of GoB’s NAP, specifically PIN5 , the IRC will build the capacity and enhance awareness among host communities and key stakeholders on climate-change and specifically on local actions taken at the community level that will help mitigate the impact of climate change and reduce disruptions on livelihoods, through the implementation of 10 Local Adaptation Plans of Actions (LAPAs). In consultation and collaboration with the local communities and local government representatives, these LAPAs will focus on climate-resilient structures and processes such as early-warning preparedness, climate-smart agriculture and resilient livelihoods and will be validated with Upazila officials to ensure alignment with the National Adaptation Plan (NAP). Once the LAPAs are validated, the project will support the identification of four of the most disruptive and recurring issues at the community level through the implementation of resilience building projects following the cash-for-work modality.
At the camp level, the IRC will similarly deliver a three-pronged approach to address the camp-level climate-induced vulnerabilities. Firstly, the IRC will deliver a training to camp disaster management committees, Community-Based Protection Committees (CBPCs), and women’s groups on how to conduct a climate risk assessment, following this, the IRC will conduct participatory climate risk mapping in targeted project locations in the camps to systematically identify vulnerabilities to climate-induced hazards such as floods, heatwaves, and cyclones and their consequences on the lives of the affected Based on the risk mapping community-led early action plans will be developed in coordination with camp management authorities, the project will prioritise four of the most disruptive and recurring climate-induced challenges and support refugee-led resilience-building projects using the cash-for-work modality, in alignment with the GoB’s guidance

Assumptions • Timely approval of FD6 and FD7 by NGOAB and approval of all needs assessment reports by Camp in Charges and UNO. • Political, peace and security situations in the camps and the host communities remains conducive for smooth implementation. • Ability and willingness of the local government authorities and the camps and host community people to participate in the project. • Rohingya refugees will continue to be allowed to attend skills-building activities
Risks • Violent incidents in the camps may increase due to clashes between armed groups, refugees and host communities, or security forces and refugee or host communities. • Upcoming national election/harsh weather can put a big challenge on organizing the project resources and delay the field level implementation. • Local authorities and stakeholders may disagree on geographical targets, guidelines or activities. • The provision of cash grants for refugee youth is yet to be formalised and officially approved by the Government of Bangladesh. • Severe monsoon weather, including flooding, erosion, and landslides, could disrupt camps and agricultural activities.
Risk Mitigation Strategy:
• Maintain close coordination with camp authorities, law enforcement, and protection actors to monitor security and respond to threats. Apply conflict-sensitive approaches and conduct regular safety assessments to ensure staff and project participants’ safety. Activities will be adjusted, paused, or relocated if violence escalates. • Develop flexible implementation and contingency plans to manage delays due to national elections or extreme weather events. Coordinate with local administration to minimize disruptions and schedule remote or indoor activities during high-risk periods. • Engage government departments, sectoral actors, and stakeholders through regular coordination meetings to build consensus, capture learnings, and ensure alignment with national policies and guidelines. • Maintain coordination with LSDS, RRRC and other relevant government authorities to advocate for formal approval of cash grants. Prepare alternative livelihood support plans, such as in-kind business inputs to ensure continuity if approvals are delayed. • Adopt flexible and adaptive planning, support community-led disaster preparedness, and prioritise cost-effective resilience interventions that can be sustained even in resource-constrained settings.

OUTCOME: Improved access to food security and livelihoods, and strengthened resilience for vulnerable host community and refugee households in Bangladesh The project is designed to deliver tangible improvements in the lives of vulnerable Rohingya refugees and host community members in Bangladesh by integrating climate resilience with economic opportunity in line with the RAF fund objectives. The core expected result is to ensure that that targeted households will become more self-reliant and better equipped to handle climate shocks through enhanced food security, diversified livelihoods, and direct participation in environmental restoration. Success will be measured by a key performance indicator including the percentage of targeted vulnerable households reporting increased income and better access to markets as a direct result of their engagement in climate-resilient agriculture or newly created green jobs.
OUTPUT 1.1: Diversified livelihood (Employment) opportunities and household resilience through skills development, asset support, and climate-smart income-generating activities. The project will directly create green job opportunities for both Rohingya and host community men and women through innovative initiatives like provision of green skills and readymade garment (RMG) industry waste recycling and bolster food security by providing climate-resilient agricultural inputs and training both general and advanced/lead farmers on adaptive and innovative agricultural techniques. Furthermore, the project aims to ensure safe and inclusive access to relevant and essential skills development opportunities for marginalised youth including people with disability, ultimately enhancing their income prospects and resilience in crisis-affected refugee and host communities. Building on the NRC youth well-being framework, the initiative will provide comprehensive support across multiple areas, including soft skills and entrepreneurship, enabling youth to transition into sustainable employment and achieve greater self-reliance.
OUTPUT 1.2: Target communities and local authorities are actively engaged in community-led climate resilience interventions through strengthened collaboration and capacity-building. The project will aim to ensure community-Led Climate Adaptation and Environmental Restoration by empowering communities to become active agents in managing their environment. The project will implement landslide slope stabilization and risk mitigation schemes using nature-based solutions. These interventions will be community-led, employing both host community and Rohingya men and women through a cash-for-work approach. Furthermore, the project will support household-level soil stabilization activities within refugee camps and build the capacity of Rohingya community members to lead and sustain these climate resilience interventions.
Reporting Against International Climate Finance (ICF) KPIs: The project's impact will be rigorously measured against the UK’s ICF framework, demonstrating its contribution to global climate goals. The key KPIs are: 1) ICF KPI 01: Number of people supported to better adapt to the effects of climate change. This will capture every individual who receives training, agricultural or livestock inputs, or participates in cash-for-work schemes, 2) ICF KPI 04: Number of people whose resilience has been improved. This measures the beneficiaries who have demonstrably increased their income or food security, making them better able to withstand climate and economic shocks. 3) ICF KPI 06: Tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions reduced or avoided. This will be quantified by calculating the GHG emissions avoided through various project interventions including, the recycling of RMG industry waste.

This project, led by NRC (consortium lead), DRC, IRC and HI, in collaboration with local partners addresses critical challenges faced by both Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, related to climate vulnerability, environmental degradation, and limited livelihood opportunities. The project is closely aligned with the RAF's core objectives to build the resilience of the most vulnerable and food- and nutrition-insecure households to shocks and stresses, particularly those driven by climate change. Operating across household, community, and systems, the project adopts a holistic, multisectoral approach to strengthen climate-resilient livelihoods, promote sustainable and nutrition-sensitive food systems, and institutionalise inclusive market interventions, ultimately enabling communities to withstand climate-driven shocks, improve food security, enhance diversified livelihood sources and reduce reliance on humanitarian aid. Additionally, the climate-risk assessments jointly developed in the refugee camps will inform the implementation of resilience-building community projects against the impact of climate-change. Youth will be trained in trades which are identified through NRC’s youth-led market assessment. Graduates will receive tailored start-up kits, cash grants, job placements, and internships, complemented by mentoring and job fairs to facilitate sustainable income generation. Handicap International (HI) will ensure the inclusivity of consortium interventions by embedding disability-inclusive approaches across climate-resilient activities and empowering learners with disabilities by developing their skills to create income-generating opportunities. The exit strategy for consortium partners will emphasise community ownership and sustainability through clear handover and capacity-building actions. Community-led initiatives such as Local Adaptation Plans, developed and validated with government stakeholders, will be integrated into local development plans. Strengthened linkages with private companies and service providers will ensure access to climate-smart technologies, soil erosion projects, and climate-resilient livelihoods will be transferred to existing community structures, camp-level Site Development focal points, CIC offices, and local government. Women and girls' groups will be equipped with skills and market linkages to maintain their livelihoods, while youth groups will be encouraged to take leadership in climate action projects. The trained Youth with disabilities will work for supply some devices for other projects of HI in this context. HI will also advocate with other agencies working in camps and sectors to utilize their skills for making some devices and assistive products for their beneficiaries specially for children. They will also continue work for repairing devices of individuals from communities. All nature-based solutions will rely on affordable, locally available resources, making them easy to replicate and sustain over time.

Why does the proposed delivery partner the right one?
The Centre for Natural Resource Studies (CNRS), an IRC partner, is a well-established NGO with 30+ years of experience in climate resilience, sustainable livelihoods, nature-based solutions, and community-based development in Bangladesh. It has a strong presence in Cox’s Bazar and close ties with both refugee and host communities.
ESDO (Eco-Social Development Organization), a DRC partner, will support RAF project implementation in Cox’s Bazar to strengthen its effectiveness, reach, and sustainability. With strong local knowledge and community trust, ESDO has proven experience working with refugees and host communities, forming CBOs, and running green job initiatives like garment waste processing.
Uttaran, a trusted NRC partner, has extensive experience in skills development for both host and displaced communities in Bangladesh. Its community-driven approach blends inclusive planning, market-relevant training, and strong stakeholder coordination. Since October 2023, Uttaran has trained 464 youths (212 host, 252 Rohingya) across six trades under the Skill Development Project.
Prottyashi (HI partner) is an experienced national NGO with strong operational presence in Cox’s Bazar. It brings proven expertise in inclusive green skills training, climate-smart agriculture, cash-for-work, and market access for vulnerable groups, including women and persons with disabilities, through adaptive programming and community-based approaches and reached over 30,000 individuals.
